newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan unwittingly votes for new political turmoIl.
newsitem.headline: Japan unwittingly votes for new political turmoIl.

text.p: Japan unwittingly voted for new political turmoil in Sunday's election when they failed to give Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's party a clear majority but also decided not to gamble on untried opposition parties.

The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was set to stay in charge as the largest party, but the shape of Hashimoto's new government -- and how it would use its mandate -- could take days or weeks to emerge.

With projections showing the LDP likely to fall short of a majority of the 500 Lower House seats at stake, the party will have to apply powers of persuasion to secure a cushion its electoral machine could not deliver.
Television network projections showed the LDP was set to win about 240 seats.

Possible LDP coalition partners include an upstart party of young reformists who would hold Hashimoto's feet to the fire on reform -- or disgruntled members of losing parties seeking comfort and safety in the ruling camp, analysts said.
Choices of partners range from its previous allies in the outgoing coalition, the Social Democrats and Sakigake, to the newly formed Democratic Party.

In an increasing likely scenario, Hashimoto may seek to ally with both the old guard Social Democrats to secure their support in the Upper House and reformists in the new Democratic Party to command the powerful Lower House.

The Social Democrats and Sakigake were decimated at the polls, after many of their members defected to the Democratic Party, which was formed last month. But the Socialists still hold a pivotal card -- 36 seats in the 252-seat Upper House.
Social Democratic leader Takako Doi was noncommittal about an alliance, saying her priority was party building.
The Democrats, who secured some 50 seats, have declined to commit to a coalition with the LDP until they receive the conservative party's promises on administrative reform.

"We have never ruled out joining the government, but the decision will depend on whether there is a high possibility of our key policies being implemented," said Naoto Kan, co-leader of the Democrats.
Such policies include streamlining government and making policy-making more transparent -- ideas to which the LDP is a late convert because of its cozy ties to bureaucrats.
Junichiro Koizumi, an outspoken senior LDP lawmaker, said sweeping governmental reform is the unavoidable policy task of whatever cabinet is formed.

Political analyst Minoru Morita said the LDP might actually be relieved about not having to form a government on its own, because with coalition partners it can share the pain and blame for tough decisions on tax policy and slashing government.
"The past two years of coalition government have actually been easy for the LDP leadership, because its partners helped take responsibility for policies," Morita told Reuters.
"It would have been a real test for the LDP to carry out its campaign pledges entirely on its own."

One LDP option -- which does not bode well for reforms -- would be to lure individual members of the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), which fared poorly on Sunday, across the aisle. Many Shinshinto members are former LDP lawmakers.

"LDP leaders know that some 20 members of Shinshinto are likely to defect or redefect to the ruling party after the elections," said political analyst Takayoshi Miyagawa of the Centre for Political Public Relations, a private think-tank.
